surfaces.part: top end strip of the barricade (yellow/red band)
sandbag rows 1 to 7, each a face-on bag with a 1-row highlight, a body and a dark bottom line (rows 4-9, 10-16, 17-23, 24-30, 31-37, 38-46)

answer.evidence: The object is a vertical stack of bag rows, each about 6-7 rows tall. Every bag is a face-on rounded block with a 1-row light highlight at its upper edge (rows 4, 18, 32, 39), a flat mid-tone body, and a dark 1-row bottom line (rows 9, 16, 23, 30, 37). The highlight is a rim, not a top plane. No bag has a band ending in a front-edge line with eave shadow below it, no ellipse, and no visible contents. The yellow/red strip at rows 0-3 is a flat band with no edge line, so it is not a convincing top surface. The repeated rows read as stacked front elevations with at most a 1-2 row rim on top, not as a 3/4 top plus front.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow sandbag column about one tile wide, set beside two much larger house references. Measured facts favour it: 15 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, 0% near-flat coverage like both references, and only 6% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outlines are tinted. By eye, each bag has a lit bulging top, a mid body, a darker front and a tinted dark edge. The bags are separated by value rather than a uniform black line. There is some grain and per-bag variation, though less than the roof tiles and plaster of the houses. The five or so shading steps per bag are slightly below the 6 on the references' main materials, but this is a small prop and is not flat or sticker-like beside them.

bag rows 5-7 (green, gray and brown bags)

answer.evidence: The drawing is a stack of bag rows, each about 6-7 rows tall. Each bag is a flat front-facing block with a small 1-2 px highlight patch and a dark bottom edge. The width profile stays at 16 with only 1-row notches between bag rows, so there is no ellipse or widen-then-narrow profile. No row band ends in a front-edge line followed by eave shadow. The only top-like element is the 2-3 row yellow/red strip at rows 0-3, which is a thin rim and not a top surface. Each bag has a bulging look but no horizontal top plane, so the structure reads as a front elevation, not three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The references are whole houses and the candidate is a narrow sandbag column, so the comparison is on material craft rather than form. Each bag has a lit bulging top, a mid tone, a darker front and a shadow seam, which gives about 5 steps per bag. The bags alternate between grey-stone, green-grey and brown tones with per-bag variation, much like the stone-wall tones on house-h112. Measured facts support this: 15 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, 0% near-flat coverage, and only 6% neutral dark edge pixels. The edges are therefore tinted dark material tones rather than a black sticker line. No large flat fills are visible. The piece is small, but a careful artist would accept it next to the reference without it looking thinner or flatter.

surfaces.part: top strip (yellow/red band along the top)

answer.evidence: The object is a vertical stack of about six sandbag courses, each 7 rows tall. In every course a lit bulging top of about 4 rows (for example rows 10-13) is followed by 2 rows of darker shade (rows 14-15) and a 1-row dark edge line (row 16). Corner rows are narrower (widths 10, 14 and 8 at the course boundaries), which gives rounded bag ends. This is a top band, then a front-edge line, then a short front, repeated. The front is short, only about 3 rows per course, so the drawing leans toward top-down. There is no roof, lintel or gate structure, so the object is a barricade rather than a large structure. The 3-row strip at rows 0-2 is a flat front-facing band with no edge line.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow column of stacked bags. Each bag has a lit bulging top, a mid-tone body and a darker short front face. This gives about 4-5 lightness steps per bag, a little below the references' 5-6. The outlines lean brown or green to match the neighbouring bag rather than forming a neutral black line, which agrees with the measured 6% near-neutral dark edge pixels (references 7-9%). Bags are separated by value changes and tinted edges. There are no flat fills: near-flat coverage is 0% and there are no 5x5 single-colour blocks. Visible tones per tile are 15, against 12 and 10 for the references, so density is at or above the references. Texture is moderate, with per-bag highlights and speckle but no extensive grain like the roof tile scallops. A careful artist would accept it next to the stone-wall reference without it looking thinner or more sticker-like.

surfaces.part: sandbag courses (stacked rows of bags, each with a tan tie highlight, body and dark bottom line)

answer.evidence: The top 2 rows (0-1, yellow then pink-red, width 14) form only a thin rim. Below, the image is a repeating stack of bag courses about 7 rows tall. Each course has a 1-row tan tie highlight, a flat colored body of brown, grey or green, and a 1-2 row dark line at its base (rows 8-9, 16-17, 23-24, 30-31, 37-38). The courses are drawn face-on, with no ellipse and no band ending in a front-edge line. The bags' bulging tops are not shown as horizontal surfaces, so the whole drawing reads as a front elevation of stacked bags.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow stack of sandbags, drawn at the reference scale. Each bag has a lit bulging top, a mid tone and a darker front, so I count about 4 lightness steps per material against roughly 5 on the references' roofs and walls. The measured facts back this up. It has 15 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references. Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as the references, so there are no flat fills. Only 6% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, which is in line with the references' 7% and 9%. By eye the outlines lean brown or green with the bag colour, not black, so I call them dark material tone. The bags are shaded one by one, much like the stones on the stone house. It is small and a prop, so the lack of roof-scallop texture is not held against it. A careful artist would accept it beside the references without it looking thinner or more sticker-like.
